transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-29
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Ortega, Daniel Kim, Ravi Patel (Redwood); Priya Shah, Luca Moretti, Amir Khan, Sofia Gomez (HavenWorks)

Summary:
Quick Optimize console walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for HavenWorks' chat assistant. Showed cost vs latency tradeoffs, demonstrated sandbox sim, and agreed on data request trace to run a precise savings model. Next steps and owners captured.

Topics covered:
- High-level econ: cost per token vs throughput SLOs
- Prefix (lookahead) KV cache heuristics and TTLs
- Batching sizing, concurrency, and tail-latency effects
- Session-affinity vs stateless routing and burst capacity
- Sandbox run & data handoff

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate) ---
[00:00] Maya Ortega: Hey team thanks for joining, I see we have Priya, Amir, Luca, Sofia from HavenWorks, hi!
[00:06] Priya Shah: Hi everyone, yeah thanks, excited. We're looking to reduce costs on our assistant while keeping p50 latency under 150ms, p95 under 300ms ideally.
[00:14] Maya Ortega: Great, that's useful. Quick intro - I'll run the Console Optimize tour and Daniel will cover the SE bits and the sandbox scripts.
[00:22] Daniel Kim: Hey all. also slight note, I may butcher some of your internal names if I misread the trace, please correct me.
[00:29] Amir Khan: No worries, go for it.

[00:45] Daniel Kim: Alright first slide is the cost model overview - think of cost as tokens-served plus fixed GPU amortization. On Redwood Optimize we show batch-size distributions and a suggested batching window. For chat-like patterns we tend to recommend a hybrid: small immediate batch for low-latency queries, combined with a slightly delayed micro-batch for tail smoothing.
[01:05] Sofia Gomez: When you say micro-batch what's the usual delay you're recommending?
[01:10] Daniel Kim: Usually 8-25ms for interactive, though it depends on your request volume. At very high concurrency you can push to 50ms and still be fine. But that increases unit token efficiency.

[03:12] Priya Shah: Our workload is bursty by hour but per-session it's short (1-3 turns), we also have a lot of repeated prefixes for the assistant context.
[03:20] Maya Ortega: That pattern is actually a great candidate for prefix/KV cache. If you have a canonical prompt prefix or system message reused a lot, the KV cache stores the key-value states per prefix and reuses them across sessions to avoid recomputing attention for the same context.
[03:38] Luca Moretti: Earlier we were thinking of naive session caching but worried about memory and eviction churn. How do you recommend sizing it?
[03:46] Ravi Patel: Good question. Two levers: TTL and cache key cardinality. In Console Optimize we provide a 'lookahead' hit-rate estimator from your sample traces. From that we pick a TTL to balance hit-rate vs memory pressure. For HavenWorks with 3k active sessions and high prefix reuse, we might start with a 10-20 minute TTL and cap entries per shard.
[04:10] Priya Shah: 10-20 minutes sounds long, is eviction cost high?
[04:14] Daniel Kim: Eviction itself is cheap, but the cost is memory and potential stale caching if your system messages change often. If you do rapid rollout of prompts, shorter TTLs or versioned prefix keys help. You can also set a small fingerprint of prompt version to avoid stale hits.

[06:00] Amir Khan: What about prefetch? We saw a note in Redwood docs about proactive prefetch for expected next-turns. Our assistant can often predict follow-ups.
[06:07] Maya Ortega: Prefetch is powerful when predictions are high-confidence. In practice, combine prefetch with a budget: decide how many tokens you are willing to speculatively compute per session. Console Optimize surface shows a spec budget metric and estimated wasted token fraction. For HavenWorks' config we'd recommend conservative prefetch (1-2 tokens) until we see the sample trace's predictability metric.

[08:30] Luca Moretti: Any easy knobs to tune from our side before we hand over traces?
[08:35] Ravi Patel: Yes: 1) Identify static prefix templates and tag them, 2) enable session-affinity routing for heavy users to increase intra-shard cache locality, 3) enable conservative KV TTLs. All of these are toggles in the Console under Optimize -> Caching.

[10:12] Sofia Gomez: Can you show the Optimize console live?
[10:17] Maya Ortega: Sure I'll share my screen. -- (screen share noise) -- okay, top right is the cost simulator, we can change per-request concurrency, batching delay, and TTL sliders.
[10:40] Daniel Kim: I'm going to load a synthetic trace we prepared similar to HavenWorks profile, note that our synthetic has shorter sessions but similar prefix reuse.
[11:05] Maya Ortega: See here, with default batch window 15ms and TTL 15m, estimated token cost reduction is 28% vs baseline. If we increase micro-batch window to 35ms the reduction goes to 41% but p95 increases by ~40ms.
[11:30] Priya Shah: p95 increases by 40ms - might be acceptable if we can keep under 300ms.
[11:34] Daniel Kim: Right, and remember you can route high-priority users to a lower-latency policy (no batching) and background traffic to cost-optimized policy. That's the per-route policy in the Console.

[13:50] Luca Moretti: What's the memory footprint for a 10-20 minute TTL for our scale, roughly?
[13:56] Ravi Patel: For our model family and 3k active sessions, ballpark 40-80GB of KV state depending on average sequence length. This is why we recommend sharding across a few dedicated nodes or using dedicated capacity with larger GPU memory when TTL grows.

[16:20] Amir Khan: If we go Hosted vs Dedicated, what differences should we expect operationally?
[16:26] Maya Ortega: Hosted is easiest — Redwood manages the cache layer; you get Optimize suggestions but less control over exact eviction policies. Dedicated gives you predictable throughput, colocated cache, and control over shard counts and memory. For HavenWorks with compliance needs you can also pick Private (VPC) and still use Console Optimize with a connected control-plane.

[18:00] Priya Shah: On the security side, we need KMS integrations and audit logs for cache hits/evictions. Do you surface audit events?
[18:10] Daniel Kim: Yes, Console retains per-request metadata and cache event logs can be exported to your SIEM via our audit export. KMS/HSM integration for model keys is supported in Private deployments. We'll share the SOC2 + security brief.

[20:30] Sofia Gomez: Could you explain how the cost model treats quantized vs non-quantized variants?
[20:36] Ravi Patel: We account for per-token GPU cost and adjust for quantized variant speed-ups. Optimize includes a model variant table with measured throughput and token cost delta. If you switch to an 8-bit quantized variant you might see 20-40% token cost reduction but watch quality regressions; console ties this to eval sets so you can gate rollouts.

[23:45] Daniel Kim: Back to batching: one gotcha is tail-latency amplification when you batch large context lengths. If user queries vary between short and long sequences, a single batch can be dominated by long ones and push p95 up. Our recommendation is to stratify batch queues by length buckets or use priority batching. Console Optimize simulates stratified batching too.
[24:10] Priya Shah: We have a long-tail of occasional long documents ( > 2048 tokens ). Should we special-case those?
[24:16] Maya Ortega: Yes - route those to a separate long-context pool or use a different model/variant. That keeps the interactive pool snappy.

[26:50] Luca Moretti: Can you run a quick scenario change: TTL to 5m, batch window 20ms, and concurrency 200?
[26:55] Daniel Kim: Switching now - okay the sim updates: cost reduction ~22%, p50 ~120ms, p95 ~280ms. Hit-rate on KV drops from 68% -> 45%. So you're trading hit-rate for fresher cache and lower mem.
[27:25] Amir Khan: 45% hit-rate is still decent. How do you measure which prefix templates get hit?
[27:30] Ravi Patel: Console has a top-k prefix heatmap and hit contributors. We can export the list of most frequent prefix fingerprints to help you consolidate templates.

[30:00] Priya Shah: On instrumentation, we'll send a 7-day request trace — what format do you prefer?
[30:06] Daniel Kim: JSONL with request timestamps, session IDs, prompt length, outcome tokens. We gave a template in the onboarding doc. If you can't send raw prompts for privacy, you can send hashed prompt fingerprints plus lengths and timestamps. That still drives accurate hit-rate and batch distribution sims.

[32:50] Maya Ortega: A short note on session-affinity: enabling it increases local hits but can reduce global batching efficiency. You can enable sticky sessions for top 20% of heavy users. That typically increases hit-rate more than it hurts batching.
[33:10] Luca Moretti: Hmm ok, that may fit our power-users.

[34:40] Sofia Gomez: Any obvious low-hanging toggles we can flip to get quick wins?
[34:45] Maya Ortega: Yes: reduce batch-window from 50ms to 20ms for interactive routes, enable KV TTL 10m for high reuse prefixes, and enable per-route fallback to a cheaper quantized model for low-priority workloads. Those three combined often net 20-35% savings quickly.

[36:15] Priya Shah: About fallbacks — how seamless is it? We worry about quality cliffs.
[36:20] Daniel Kim: Console supports canary rollouts with automatic quality checks based on your eval set. If the quantized variant degrades quality beyond your threshold we auto-fallback. You can also set soft rollouts (percent traffic) and monitor t-tests on eval metrics.

[38:40] Maya Ortega: We're going to propose a pilot: Redwood runs the sandbox with your 7-day trace, we simulate three policies (low-latency, balanced, cost-optimized) and deliver a short report. Sound good?
[38:50] Priya Shah: Yes, that helps. Timeline?
[38:53] Maya Ortega: If you send traces by Apr 5, we can run within a week and present results Apr 13-15.

[40:10] Luca Moretti: About dedicated nodes: what's minimum capacity to avoid noisy neighbor effects?
[40:16] Ravi Patel: For our model family typical minimum is 4 GPU pods for dedicated capacity to get stable throughput at your scale; you can start with a smaller commit if you accept autoscale bursts. Dedicated has predictable queues and local cache.

[42:55] Amir Khan: Any regulatory concerns with caching user context? We need PII minimization.
[43:02] Daniel Kim: You can opt out of caching for routes that may contain PII, or filter/normalize content before storing. Console has routing rules to disable caching on specific intents or tags. We'll share best-practices doc.

[45:20] Sofia Gomez: Ok final recap and next actions please?
[45:25] Maya Ortega: Recap - Redwood to run sandbox sim once HavenWorks provides 7-day trace (or fingerprinted pgp) by Apr 5, Maya will share the cost model sheet by Apr 1, Daniel will prepare the sandbox script and run canary scenarios by Apr 10. We recommended initial config: TTL 10m, batch window 20ms, enable session-affinity for top users, conservative prefetch (1 token).
[46:00] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Please also send the security brief and SOC2 link.
[46:06] Maya Ortega: Will do.

[47:30] (Short side conversation, audio overlap)
[48:10] Luca Moretti: One extra Q - how do you recommend we version prefix keys when templates evolve?
[48:16] Ravi Patel: Add a prompt-template version tag to the cache key (small integer). Console's SDK includes a helper to compute key fingerprints and attach a version. That lets you rotate templates without mass eviction.

[50:40] Priya Shah: If we want to move to Dedicated later, can we preserve cache state or is it rebuilt?
[50:46] Daniel Kim: You can export cache state snapshots and import into the new dedicated pool; there will be a warm-up, but snapshot/import is supported for Private/Dedicated migrations.

[52:10] Maya Ortega: Alright, thanks everyone, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security docs.
[52:18] Priya Shah: Thanks all.
[52:20] Amir Khan: Thanks.
[52:21] Sofia Gomez: Thanks, bye.

(Recording ends ~16:54 UTC)
